patient_information: A 23-year-old Zambian woman recently diagnosed with HIV infection one month prior to presentation. She is not yet on antiretroviral therapy (ART) but has been taking co-trimoxazole prophylaxis for the last seven days. Her CD4 count is noted to be low. She has a past medical history of pulmonary tuberculosis, which was successfully treated four years ago. She works in a hospital cafeteria, does not drink alcohol or use recreational drugs.
history_of_present_illness: The patient experienced her first-ever seizure, which occurred out of sleep. A family member found her on the floor, unresponsive and shaking all four limbs for a duration of 5 to 10 minutes.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient is from Lusaka, Zambia and works in a hospital cafeteria. No other specific exposures or travel history are mentioned.
vitals: On examination, her vital signs were normal and she was afebrile.
physical_exam: The patient appeared well with a GCS of 15/15. There was no meningism and her chest was clear. The neurological examination was unremarkable.
labs_and_diagnostics: A malaria rapid diagnostic test was negative. Blood results showed a WBC of 5.8 x 10^9/L and hemoglobin of 11.0 g/dL. A lumbar puncture was performed with a normal opening pressure. The CSF was clear with 0 leukocytes/μL, a raised protein of 0.78 g/L, and normal glucose. CSF tests for Cryptococcal antigen (CrAG), India Ink, Gram stain, and Ziehl–Neelsen stain were all negative. A CT scan of her brain revealed frontal and parietal hypodense lesions in the white matter of the right hemisphere with no contrast enhancement. An EEG demonstrated focal slowing in the right hemisphere. JC-virus DNA was later detected in the CSF as part of a research study.
differential_diagnosis: The differential diagnosis for focal brain lesions in an HIV-positive patient with new-onset seizure included tuberculoma, progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML), cerebral toxoplasmosis, cryptococcoma, brain abscess, primary CNS lymphoma, and neurocysticercosis. The CT findings of lesions selectively affecting the white matter without contrast enhancement or perifocal oedema were considered strongly suggestive of PML.
management_and_clinical_course: The patient was started on carbamazepine 200mg twice daily for seizure prevention. She was also commenced on antiretroviral therapy (ART) to manage the underlying condition. After six months, she remained seizure-free and carbamazepine was discontinued. One year after starting ART, her CD4 count had recovered to 535 cells/μL and she had returned to work.
final_diagnosis: The final diagnosis was progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML). This was suspected based on the clinical presentation of a new-onset seizure in a patient with advanced immunosuppression from HIV, and characteristic neuroimaging showing non-enhancing hypodense lesions in the subcortical white matter. The diagnosis was later confirmed by the detection of JC-virus DNA in the cerebrospinal fluid.
